newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean economy in serious trouble - minister.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean economy in serious trouble - minister.

text.p: Finance minister Kang Kyong-shik said on Thursday that South Korea's economy was in serious trouble, battered by bankruptcies, a month of labour strikes and a political crisis.
"There is no doubt the Korean economy is currently in serious trouble," he told a news conference.
Kang said the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co in January, labour unrest and a related political crisis had "all added more uncertainties and instability in the economy".

He said much of South Korea's current account deficit was due to a sharp downturn in the terms of trade, fuelled by plunging prices of exports, including semiconductors. The deficit hit an all-time high of $23.72 billion last year.
"The fear is that there may be a further decline in the balance of payments as the economy's structural problems take a toll on the country's international competitiveness," Kang said.
Kang, who took over as minister of finance and economy in a cabinet reshuffle last month, said to overcome the problems it was crucial to "refrain from trying to stimulate the economy any time soon".
He said the government was grappling with "high-cost and low-efficiency" that has been nurtured by heavy-handed government regulation and has plagued the economy.
"What is called for is deregulation and promotion of competition," he added. The government would speed up financial sector reform.
Kang also expressed hope that a new labour law which came into force last month would foster more flexible labour relations.
Kang noted the government planned to slash two trillion won ($2.2 billion) from this year's budget and lower tax revenue by equivalent amount to help reduce overall demand in the economy.
Fiscal tightening would be maintained next year to keep budget spending to a single digit.
Energy prices will remain high to encourage conservation and reduce imports. Energy imports have been a major factor behind a balooning trade deficit.
Referring to moves announced this week to open the local stock and bond markets wider to foreigners and expand overseas borrowings, Kang said the goal was financial market stability.
"The Korean government will take all necessary steps to ensure stability in the domestic financial market, and further to ensure Korea's credibility in the international financial market," Kang said.
He said he was confident South Korea would weather the storm, noting that the country's economy had passed through "one crisis after another" since the early 1960s.
"So long as this crisis lasts we will be forced to give up our complacency for painful efforts to overcome the current situion," he said.
